headlines.article_text: Tech giants face more child safety suits while pushing AI in schools Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Social media companies are dealing with more child safety lawsuits at the same time that the industry is trying to push AI deeper into classrooms. Snap reached a settlement with two plaintiffs this week, days before a scheduled trial over allegations that its product contributed to harmful behavior. Developmental psychologist Kate Blocker said products need "broader systemic changes in tech design, particularly when children are using them." In this article GEMI SNAP META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Didem Mente | Anadolu | Getty Images Tech companies have spent years telling parents they're working to make their products safer for children. But ongoing jury trials, settlements and related litigation against the likes of Meta , Google and Snap suggest that they're not doing enough. The latest examples landed this week. Snap confidentially settled a case claiming that its technology caused severe psychological distress to two teenage users. Meta , TikTok and YouTube previously settled with the plaintiffs in the same suit. And Google was sued this week by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with the Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom. Concern is intensifying as artificial intelligence companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations, and established internet giants pour money into developing advanced AI models while pushing them into the classroom. Products and features intended to maximize engagement can have detrimental effects on users, thus warranting "broader systemic changes in tech design, particularly when children are using them," said developmental psychologist Kate Blocker. "I think it's so so important that children's safety is being considered when these products — AI, social media, et cetera — are being designed, and not after the fact as these problems emerge," said Blocker, the director of research and programs for the nonprofit Children and Screens.
